title: Robert D. Hare Lifetime Achievement Award
source: Society for the Scientific Study of Psychopathy
html: Kent Kiehl received the 2026 Robert D. Hare Lifetime Achievement Award, the highest honor of the Society for the Scientific Study of Psychopathy (SSSP).

title: “Ed Kemper: Inside the Mind of a Psychopath” on UNMARKED
html: Dr. Kiehl was the guest on Episode 44 of UNMARKED: A True Crime Podcast. The episode is on YouTube, Apple Podcasts and Audioboom.

title: Keynote at CrimeCon 2026 in Las Vegas
html: Dr. Kiehl gave an invited keynote, “What makes them tick? Inside the mind of a psychopath,” at CrimeCon 2026 at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas. About 6,000 people attended the conference.

title: The Psychopath Whisperer: rights sold in India
html: Rights to The Psychopath Whisperer were sold in India in 2026. The book has been published in North America and the United Kingdom and translated into Chinese, Dutch, Finnish, German, Polish, Russian and Turkish. About the book.

title: “Meet the Neuroscientist Who Has Scanned Over 5000 Psychopathic Brains!”
html: A two-hour interview with Dr. Kiehl on the Giant’s Shoulder podcast.

title: Ask the Expert: Dr. Kent Kiehl
html: A written question-and-answer session for the Aftermath: Surviving Psychopathy Foundation.

title: Ethics Grand Rounds at the UNM Health Sciences Center
html: Dr. Kiehl’s lecture for the Institute for Ethics at the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center.

title: “L’uomo che viaggia nel cervello dei killer. ‘Così nasce una mente criminale’”
html: International press: Eleonora Mancini’s article in the Italian newspaper Quotidiano Nazionale.

title: “Skeptically Curious,” Episode 13: The Psychopath Whisperer with Dr. Kent Kiehl (Part 1)
html: Ryan Rutherford interviews Dr. Kent Kiehl in Episode 13 of the podcast Skeptically Curious. Listen on Spotify or Apple Podcasts.

title: The Story of God with Morgan Freeman
html: Morgan Freeman visits Illinois serial killer Brian Dugan for his documentary series. In an episode examining the concept of evil, Freeman’s production company worked with neuroscientist Kent Kiehl, author of The Psychopath Whisperer, who uses clinical brain imaging to better understand major mental illnesses, with a specific focus on criminal psychopathy.

title: “The Brain, the Criminal and the Courts”
html: An article by Eryn Brown in The Fix, January 2020.

title: Psychology and neuroscience professor explains conduct disorders
html: Dr. Kiehl on Megyn Kelly TODAY, NBC.

title: “The Science of Good and Evil”
html: National Geographic’s feature article included the Kiehl laboratory’s brain-imaging research.

title: “A Peek Inside a Murderer’s Brain”
html: CNN reports on the laboratory’s brain-imaging studies of people who have committed homicide.

title: “New Mexico Study Aims to Unlock the Brains of Murderers, Prevent Violence”
html: 4 Investigates, KOB 4 Albuquerque.

title: “Suffering Souls: The search for the roots of psychopathy”
html: John Seabrook’s article in The New Yorker (November 10, 2008) describes Dr. Kent Kiehl’s work at the Western New Mexico Correctional Facility, where he uses MRI to scan prison inmates for signs of psychopathy in the hope of discovering a treatment.

title: “The mind of a murderer: MRI scans reveal key differences in the gray matter of homicide offenders’ brains”
html: A study mapping the brains of violent criminals is giving researchers new insight into the minds of murderers, which experts say may help predict violent behavior. Some warn it could lead to harmful profiling.

title: “Scientists studied the brains of more than 800 prisoners. Here’s what they found.”
html: Brain scans of incarcerated men reveal reduced gray matter in homicide offenders.

title: “The brain, the criminal and the courts”
html: States of mind that the legal system cares about (memory, responsibility and mental maturity) have long been difficult to describe objectively, but neuroscientists are starting to detect patterns. Coming soon to a courtroom near you?

title: “Kids serving decades for violent crimes”
html: About three dozen New Mexicans are incarcerated for 30 years or more for crimes they committed as minors. A growing body of science argues that young brains are not fully developed and, by implication, that children should be held to a different standard than adults.

title: “It’s All in the Mind Y’know: Uses and Misuses of Neuroscience in Law”
html: A discussion at the Exploratorium in San Francisco: Dr. Kent Kiehl, David Faigman and Professor Amanda Pustilnik on the challenges posed by the use of contemporary neuroscience in the courtroom. Is neuroscience ready for courtroom use? Does brain imaging permit us to measure a person’s feelings, thoughts and intentions? Can jurors understand and effectively weigh neuroscientific evidence?

title: Dr. Kiehl’s interview with All About Psychology
html: David Webb of All About Psychology had an in-depth interview with Dr. Kiehl about his research, ranging from how psychopathy research has changed over the past 20 years to the development of new treatments.

title: The Psychopath Whisperer voted psychology book of the month, February 2015
html: David Webb of All About Psychology named The Psychopath Whisperer the psychology book of the month for February 2015.

title: “What is it like to be a Psychopath?”
html: Read and listen to Dr. Kiehl’s interview with Scott Barry Kaufman of Scientific American: why psychopathy fascinates, the definition of a “true” psychopath, Dr. Kiehl’s career and his interactions with psychopaths. The podcast is on The Psychology Podcast.

title: “Mapping Criminal Minds”
html: Nicole Brady of KOB-TV interviewed Dr. Kent Kiehl about his research with thousands of inmate volunteers, analyzing differences between psychopathic and non-psychopathic brains.

title: “Researcher: Brains of dangerous youth underdeveloped”
html: Nancy Laflin of KOAT Channel 7 News interviewed Dr. Kent Kiehl about his research with juveniles. Dr. Kiehl and his team at the Mind Research Network found that the brains of youth who commit violent crimes are structured differently from those of youth with a non-violent background, differences that suggest development delayed by five to ten years.

title: “School Shooters: The First Step in Protection, Who Are They?”
html: In Forbes, prosecutor Marcia Clark comments on the nation’s epidemic of school shootings and the relationship between psychopathy and violent behavior. Clark cites Dr. Kent Kiehl and The Psychopath Whisperer, and points out that the treatment program discussed in the book may be one of the best chances for early detection and intervention for youth on a trajectory towards violence.

title: “Why Female Psychopaths Are a Different Breed”
html: Katherine Ramsland references Dr. Kent Kiehl in this article. Callous and opportunistic, female psychopaths are the rarest of a rare breed. Though they share much with their male counterparts, they may be even better equipped to elude detection.

title: “Was John Wilkes Booth a Psychopath?”
html: Writer Ross Pomeroy investigates whether the infamous assassin John Wilkes Booth was a psychopath, working through the Hare Psychopathy Checklist item by item with Dr. Kent Kiehl’s book The Psychopath Whisperer as his guide.

title: “Kent Kiehl’s Book The Psychopath Whisperer Explains the Calculating Killers Among Us”
html: Paul Teetor’s article in LA Weekly describes Dr. Kent Kiehl as the world’s leading authority on psychopaths. The piece discusses The Psychopath Whisperer, misconceptions about psychopaths and their personality traits, and psychopathy versus psychosis.

title: “One Frustration”: Russian translation in Esquire
html: John Seabrook’s article was translated into Russian. It gives a short account of Dr. Kent Kiehl’s life, his research with psychopaths and his studies of prisoners inside high-security prisons.

title: New research reveals brain differences in youth who commit homicide
html: The University of New Mexico Newsroom wrote about a study by Dr. Kent Kiehl at the Mind Research Network in Albuquerque. The study found that youth aged 12 to 18 who commit homicide have very different brains from other serious juvenile offenders who have not committed a homicide.

title: Are psychopaths impaired in their ability to make moral decisions?
html:
CNN’s article of March 26, 2014 on moral decision-making cites a few of our favorite scientists in the field of psychopathy. It raises a number of important issues, but one is central to our field: are psychopaths impaired in their ability to make moral decisions?

The short answer is: it depends.

There is ample evidence that psychopaths, compared to the rest of us, commit more moral wrongs in all domains of life. They are more likely to commit crimes, to be unfaithful, to cheat on taxes, to not pay bills, to borrow money from friends and family and never pay it back, to cheat on tests in school, and to steal from employers. To an observer, psychopaths have serious problems making appropriate moral decisions, and it makes sense that their moral abilities must be impaired.

However, when you get a psychopath into the laboratory (always be careful with them in such settings), they appear to pass the moral decision-making tasks that scientists give them. Ask a psychopath whether a picture depicts a moral wrong, and they get the answer right most of the time. Ask a psychopath to decide whether a vignette depicts a moral violation, and they get it right.

Thus, psychopaths present a conundrum: they appear to know how to act morally, but they just don’t act that way in the real world.

The answer may lie in some of the latest neuroscience of moral decision-making. Brain imaging shows that moral decision-making involves both cognitive and emotional regions of the brain. When most of us face an important moral decision, the process activates emotional systems in addition to cognitive ones. These emotional systems help to make sure we are paying attention to the importance of the decision before us.

Recent forensic studies show that these emotional brain regions are not working properly in psychopaths. Some scientists have said that psychopaths “know the words but not the music.” That is, psychopaths understand that they are making a decision, but the emotion associated with making that moral decision is lost upon them.

A study from my laboratory, led by Dr. Carla Harenski, found that criminal psychopaths had deficits in the amygdala and orbital frontal cortex when processing moral pictures, two brain regions critical for emotional processing (Harenski et al., Aberrant neural processing of moral violations in criminal psychopaths).

So, whereas psychopaths appear to be able to make moral decisions in the laboratory, the emotional systems that help govern behavior in the real world are impaired. For more on this issue, read The Psychopath Whisperer: The Science of Those Without Conscience.
